# HMS Hyperion (1807)

HMS Hyperion was a 32‑gun fifth‑rate frigate of the Royal Navy, built by contract at Kingston upon Hull and launched on 3 November 1807 to a design by Surveyor of the Navy Sir John Henslow . She served during the Napoleonic Wars and in the postwar period on multiple stations, including the Mediterranean, Jamaica/North American and West Indies Stations, and the South America and West Indies Stations. Hyperion’s recorded operations include convoy protection, anti‑piracy patrols, and prize actions, notably the recapture of the Portuguese ship Providencia (11 December 1813) and the capture of the American privateer brig Rattlesnake (June 1814) . She was paid off in 1831 and broken up in 1833 . The vessel is distinct from later Royal Navy ships named Hyperion, including the H‑class destroyer H97 that served in 1939–1940 .

## Design and construction

Hyperion was a fifth‑rate, ship‑rigged frigate of nominally 32 guns, built under contract at Kingston upon Hull (Yorkshire) and launched on 3 November 1807 . Her design is credited to Sir John Henslow, with William Gibson listed as the constructor responsible for her building at Hull . The hull was ordered on 13 June 1805 and her keel was laid in February 1806, marking a typical mid‑Napoleonic War timeline for frigate construction .

Commissioning details, tonnage (bm), dimensions, draught, and complement figures are not specified in the sources cited here; contemporary technical particulars for frigates of this rating and period are documented in standard reference works but are not independently verified in the accessible records used for this article.

## Armament and modifications

- Nominal armament: 32 guns (fifth‑rate frigate classification) .
- Equipment modification: A Plymouth Dockyard plan records “Captain Chasman’s method of stoppering chain cables” as fitted to Hyperion, signed by Edward Churchill, Master Shipwright, indicating the fitting of chain‑cable stoppering arrangements during her service life .

No detailed refit armament changes are specified in the cited sources; armament arrangements typical of the class and period are not included here unless directly sourced.

## Commanders

The following commanding officers and dates are recorded in compiled service lists and contemporary notices:

- Captain Thomas C. Brodie: in command by mid‑1808; died at Jamaica in March 1811 .
- Captain William Pryce Cumby: from September 1811; in command through 1814 .
- Captain James Lillicrap: from January 1815 (temporary/acting) .
- Captain Thomas Searle: from September 1818; South America Station .
- Captain James Lillicrap: from April 1821; Cape of Good Hope and West Indies .
- Captain George Rich: from October 1823; Jamaica Station .
- Captain William J. Mingaye: from January 1825; Coast Blockade (Newhaven) .

Subordinate officers named in action reports include First Lieutenant James Morgan and Lieutenant George Bissett during the Gonaïves incident (1811) .

## Service history

### Early deployment and Jamaica Station

- 1808: Fitted out and sailed for the Mediterranean on 30 June under Captain T. C. Brodie .
- 1810–1811: On the Jamaica Station; an incident at Gonaïves, Saint‑Domingue (Haiti), saw shore batteries fire on Hyperion’s boats, resulting in casualties and the temporary detention ashore of senior officers, resolved the next morning by bringing the frigate close inshore and issuing an ultimatum for their release (see Notable actions) .
- 1811: Command passed to Captain William Pryce Cumby in September; subsequent service confirms Hyperion’s stationing on the North American and West Indies Station (logs for 1811–1813 are catalogued by the National Archives) .

### North American and convoy service

- 1812–1813: Reported on the banks of Newfoundland and engaged in convoy duties between Newfoundland, Barbados, and British ports; weather‑dispersed convoys and damaged ships forced arrivals at Plymouth and Portsmouth at various dates late in 1813 .
- 11 December 1813: Hyperion re‑captured the Portuguese ship Providencia and cargo; the London Gazette recorded the admiralty‑prize and salvage accounting, naming Captain William Pryce Cumby, with proceeds to be deposited in the Registry of the High Court of Admiralty and Greenwich Hospital .

### 1814 operations and War of 1812 prize

- March–May 1814: Movements recorded include preparations for troop convoys towards the Garonne and carriage of specie to Bordeaux .
- June 1814: Captured the American privateer brig Rattlesnake. Secondary sources report differing dates—3 June and 14 June 1814—and record that the prize was taken into Plymouth in July; contemporary American and British notices attribute 16 nominal guns to Rattlesnake, with later tallies noting 18 guns and about 50 men at capture . The capture is widely listed among Hyperion’s wartime prizes .

Hyperion continued patrols into early 1815, after which she was paid off and laid up in ordinary at Portsmouth on 31 August 1815 .

### Postwar deployments

- 1819–1821 (South America Station): Arrived at Rio de Janeiro from Plymouth (24 October 1819) and was at Valparaíso by August 1820. Admiralty orders in October 1820 authorized detentions under anti‑slave trade treaties on the station . Hyperion paid off on 25 April 1821 and was recommissioned the same month under Captain James Lillicrap .
- 1821–1823 (Cape of Good Hope and West Indies): Conveyed Lord Charles Somerset, the Cape Governor, arriving via Madeira; recorded rescue of the Honourable East India Company’s extra ship Albion on 10 June 1822, with subsequent awards to Hyperion’s officers and crew, and further anti‑piracy cruises off Cuba, including delivering suspected pirates to Kingston, Jamaica, in December 1822 .
- 1823–1824 (Jamaica Station): Under Captain George Rich, with continued West Indies service; the ship subsequently returned to Britain for repair and reassessment .
- 1825–1831 (Coast Blockade): Stationed at Newhaven, Sussex, for anti‑smuggling duties under Captain William J. Mingaye as part of the Coast Blockade arrangements .

## Notable actions

- Gonaïves incident (Saint‑Domingue/Haiti, 1811): Contemporary accounts in service compilations record that Hyperion’s boats were fired upon by shore batteries at Gonaïves, killing three seamen and resulting in the detention ashore of Captain Brodie and others. At dawn, First Lieutenant James Morgan brought Hyperion through an intricate channel and anchored in four fathoms, close to shore; Lieutenant George Bissett was sent ashore to inform the commandant that unless the officers were set at liberty within fifteen minutes, the town would be destroyed. The detained officers were released following the ultimatum .
- Recapture of Providencia (11 December 1813): The London Gazette recorded the recapture of the Portuguese ship Providencia by Hyperion, naming Captain William Pryce Cumby and the prize agents, and directed that salvage proceeds and Greenwich Hospital shares be accounted in the Registry of the High Court of Admiralty .
- Capture of Rattlesnake (June 1814): Hyperion captured the American privateer brig Rattlesnake in June 1814; sources differ on the exact date (3 or 14 June). Rattlesnake was brought into Plymouth in July and was later sold into mercantile service; the Three Decks entry notes 18 guns and 50 men at capture in British reports .

## Incidents and records

- Prize court and salvage: The London Gazette provides the official admiralty accounting for Hyperion’s recapture of Providencia, including the allocation to Greenwich Hospital, demonstrating prize‑court procedure and distribution in late 1813/early 1814 .
- Logs and archival holdings: The National Archives Discovery catalogue records a Hyperion logbook covering 1811–1813 (North American and West Indies Station), held by the Royal Military College of Canada (Massey Library), with guidance to R. Morriss’s Guide to British Naval Papers in North America .

No courts martial or formal inquiries are directly cited in the accessible records used here.

## Fate

Hyperion was paid off and laid up in ordinary at Portsmouth in May–August 1831 after completing Coast Blockade service, and was broken up in June 1833 .

## Legacy

- Ship name: Hyperion is among several Royal Navy vessels to bear the name. A later ship of the same name was HMS Hyperion (H97), an H‑class destroyer that served in 1939–1940 and was lost off Cape Bon; the destroyer’s record is distinct and should not be conflated with the 1807 frigate .
- Material culture: A Plymouth Dockyard plan for Hyperion records a chain‑cable stoppering method fitted to the ship; the plan is signed by Edward Churchill, Master Shipwright, and survives as a technical illustration of equipment fitted to the frigate .
- Archival footprint: Hyperion’s logs for 1811–1813 survive in an overseas repository noted by the National Archives Discovery service, evidencing her North American and West Indies service .

## See also

- Royal Navy fifth‑rate frigates of the Napoleonic era.
- Prize law and the High Court of Admiralty during the Age of Sail.

## Notes on identity and disambiguation

This article covers the frigate launched in 1807. It does not address other vessels named Hyperion (including non‑naval craft and the H‑class destroyer), which are separately documented in their own records .

H-Class Fleet Destroyer ordered from Swan Hunter, Wallsend under 1934 Programme on 13th December 1934. The ship was laid down on 26th March 1935 and launched on 8th April 1936 as the 2nd RN ship to carry this name, previously used for a 5th Rate In 1807. Her build completed on 3rd December 1936 at a cost of £255,461.10s, excluding Admiralty supplied items such as guns, ammunition and signalling outfits. Her service prior to WW2 was with the 2nd Destroyer Flotilla, Mediterranean Fleet and included Non-intervention patrol duties during the Spanish Civil War. B a t t l e   H o n o u r s ATLANTIC 1939 - CALABRIA 1940 - SPADA 1940 - LIBYA  1940 - MEDITERRANEAN 1940 H e r a l d i c   D a t a Badge: On a  Field White, a Sun Red,  bordered Gold. M o t t o Fulget virtus in arduis :  'Valour shines under difficulties’ D e t a i l s   o f  W a r  S e r v i c e _(for more ship information,  go to [Naval History Homepage](https://www.naval-history.net/index.htm) and type name in Site Search)_ 1 9 3 9 August                  Arrived at Portsmouth for refit. 16th        Refit restricted to essential repairs. 27th        On completion took passage to Freetown for convoy defence. September 3rd          On passage to take up war station at Freetown. 4th          Deployed for patrol duty, trade protection and search for blockade runners and commerce raiders in South Atlantic. October                  Freetown deployment in continuation including escort of major units organised in Hunting Groups for interception of commerce raiders active in Atlantic. November              Transferred to Bermuda for patrol and escort duty in Caribbean area. Established blockade to prevent German mercantiles leaving ports in Mexico and USA. December              Caribbean deployment in continuation. 19th        Intercepted German liner COLUMBUS (32,950 CRT) off Cape Hatteras during passage to Germany. Approached when clear of American water-sand promptly scuttled. (Note: Movements of the German ship had been reported by US Navy 1 9 4 0 January                  Nominated for return to UK and took passage to Portsmouth. 25th        Taken in hand for refit by HM Dockyard, Portsmouth. February                Under refit. March                    Post refit trials. 6th          On completion took passage to Scapa Flow to rejoin 2nd Flotilla for service for screening of Home Fleet major units and patrol duties in NW Approaches. 31st         Nominated with HM Destroyer HERO for simulated minelay operation off Bud, North Norway as Force WB (Operation WILFRED). April 5th          Sailed from Scapa Flow as escort for HM Battlecruiser RENOWN during passage to Norwegian waters. 6th          Detached to refuel at Sullom Voe. 7th          Passage to Bud in heavy weather. 8th          Carried out simulated minelay. Remained in area to warn shipping until Safety patrol taken over by Norwegian warship SLEIPNER. 9th          Returned to Sullom Voe to refuel and took passage to rejoin Fleet off Narvik. 10th        Deployed as escort to Fleet units off Norway. 11th        Escorted HM Cruiser CALCUTTA with HM Destroyer ESCORT during tow of the damaged0 destroyer HMS ECLIPSE to UK 14th        Rejoined Fleet off Norway for screening duty and support to shore operations. 23rd        Deployed with HM Destroyers HEREWARD, HASTY, FEARLESS, FURY and JUNO as screen for HM Aircraft Carriers GLORIOUS and ARK ROYAL, H M Cruisers BERWICK and CURLEW during passage to carry cut Carrier Group operations off Norway (Operation DX). 24th        Rejoined Fleet on arrival. 27th        Escorted HMS ARK ROYAL during Carrier operations when HMS GLORIOUS detached. (For details of the disastrous operations in Norway see NARVIK by D. Macintyre, THE DOOMED EXPEDITION by J Adams. CARRIER GLORIOUS by J Winton, NORWAY 1940 by F Kersaudy, ENGAGE THE ENEMY MORE CLOSELY by C Barnett and Naval Staff History (HMSO-2001). May                        Took part in evacuation operations from Andalsnes and Molde. 4th          Returned to Scapa Flow on completion of evacuation deployment. 7th          Transferred to Nore Command for patrol and escort duty. 9th          Assisted in evacuation of British nationals and refugees from Hook of Holland. 12th        Nominated to escort HM Destroyer CODRINGTON for passage to UK with Dutch Royal family from Holland (Operation J) (Note: This was later cancelled ). 16th        Transferred with ships of Flotilla for Fleet duty in Mediterranean. 30th        Deployed with Flotilla at Alexandria for screening of major Fleet units. June                        Mediterranean Fleet screening duties based at Alexandria in continuation. (For details of operations in the Mediterranean after the entry of Italy in WW2 see THE BATTLE FOR THE MEDITERRANEAN by Donald MacIntyre, ENGAGE THE ENEMY MORE CLOSELY and Naval Staff History (HMSO-2002). July 7th          Part of screen for HM Aircraft Carrier EAGLE, HM Battleships MALAYA, WARSPITE, and ROYAL SOVEREIGN, HM Cruisers GLOUCESTER, LIVERPOOL, NEPTUNE, ORION and SYDNEY (RAN) with HM Destroyers DAINTY, DEFENDER, HASTY, HOSTILE, ILEX, IMPERIAL, JANUS, JUNO, VAMPIRE (RAN), and VOYAGER (RAN) to provide cover for passage of convoys MF1/MS1 to and from Malta (Operation MA5) .                               (Note: This was a repeat of Operation MA3 which had been cancelled following an engagement with Italian cruisers. See above references). 9th          Participated in engagement with Italian Fleet off Punta Stilo. (Battle of Calabria - See above references). 14th        Returned to Alexandria with Fleet. 16th        Detached with HM Destroyers HASTY, HERO and ILEX to carry cut an anti-submarine search in an area north of Crete. 19th        In action with two Italian cruisers which were then engaged by HMS SYDNEY (RAN) already deployed in the area. In subsequent attacks Italian cruiser BARTOLOMEO COLLEONI was disabled. Wreck was sunk by torpedoes from HYPERION and ILEX. (Battle of Cape Spada - See above references). .                               Rescued some survivors from BARTOLOMEO COLLEONI. August                  Fleet screening and escort duties in eastern Mediterranean in continuation. to                            (Note: Reinforcement of Fleet at Alexandria was carried cut during September. October                  (Operation HATS) and Malta convoys exchanged (Operation MB3). See above references) November 6th          Deployed with HM Destroyers DECOY, DEFENDER, HASTY, HAVOCK, HEREWARD, HERO, ILEX, JANUS, JERVIS, JUNO, MOHAWK and NUBIAN as screen for HM Battleships MALAYA, VALIANT, RAMILLIES AND WARSPITE, HM Aircraft Carrier ILLUSTRIOUS, HM Cruisers AJAX., ORION, GLOUCESTER and SYDNEY (RAN) to provide Distant Cover for passage of Convoy MW3 to Malta and Convoy ME3 to Alexandria (Operation MB8) (Note: This was part of a major operation to pass further reinforcement ships including HM Battleship BARHAM to the Fleet at Alexandria. (Operation COAT - See above references). 14th        Returned to Alexandria with Fleet. 25th        Deployed with Fleet screen 24th        Deployed with screen for HM Battleship MALAYA and m Cruiser BERWICK to provide cover for passage of convoy to Suda Bay (Operation MB9). (Note: Part of Operation COLLAR which included an air attack on Rhodes by HMS ILLUSTRIOUS and the transfer of HM Cruisers MANCHESTER and SOUTHAMPTON to join Mediterranean Fleet at Alexandria. Did not take part in the action with Italian battle group. Battle of Spartivento. See DESTROYER LEADER by P Smith and references as above). 29th        Passage to Alexandria with Fleet units. December              Deployed for support of military operation by 8th Army. Carried out bombardments. 14th        Participated in sinking of Italian submarine NAIADE off Bardia with HMS HEREWARD. 16th        Joined Force F as escort for HM Battleship MALAYA and ships of Convoy MW 5 with Destroyer ILEX for passage to Malta. (Operation MC2 - Part of Operation HIDE -See references above) .                               (Note: HMS MALAYA was being transferred to Gibraltar. Convoy comprised supply ships DEVIS, HOEGH HOOD, LANARKSHIRE, PONTFIELD, RODI, TROCAS, VOLO and WAIWERA). 20th        Under attack by Italian submarine SERPENTE which failed. (Note: Italian reports claimed sinking of this ship)) Supply ships detached to enter Malta and ss CLAN FORGES and CLAN FRASER joined HMS MALAYA in Force F from Malta to take passage to Gibraltar. Escort augmented by HM Destroyer HERO, HASTY AND HEREWARD from Fleet screen. 21st         Detached from mercantiles when escort taken over by HM Destroyers DUNCAN, JAGUAR ENCOUNTER and ISIS after passage through Sicilian Narrows. 22nd       Took passage through Narrows with HMS JERVIS and HMS ILEX Ship struck mine off Cape Bon and sustained major structural damage. Two attempts by HMS ILEX to tow were unsuccessful and ship's company taken on board HMS ILEX. Since tow clear of the area could not be accomplished before dawn and would be in sight of Pantelleria, ship was sunk by HM Destroyer JANUS in position 37.04N 11.31E. Two of the ship's company were not accounted for and reported missing presumed killed. (Note: The mine was laid in Field 4AN between Cape Bon and Pantelleria on 7th October by Italian destroyers Casualty List was published on 30 June 1941.) * * * **Addendum** **CONVOY ESCORT MOVEMENTS of HMS HYPERION** by Don Kindell _This convoy list has not been cross-checked with the text above_
